title: Occam's Razor to the Rescue
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Harriett Janetos responds to a colleague's objection that reading instruction cannot be simple because learners differ. She distinguishes the complexity of children's lives from the subject matter being taught and argues that the underlying reading process is highly similar across readers, citing Dehaene, Dylan Wiliam and Robert Pondiscio. From that she argues for streamlined, routine-based foundational instruction that frees time for other literacy components and for social-emotional growth. Drawing on Anita Archer and Marnie Ginsberg, she warns that overteaching science-of-reading content raises cognitive load and overwhelms teachers with 800-page sourcebooks. She ends by urging agreement on the essentials, the stuff rather than the fluff.
points: Children's circumstances are complicated, but because all brains learn to connect symbols with sounds in similar ways, the instruction itself can and should be simple.
Teacher training in the science of reading risks overloading both teachers and students; knowing all of the language science does not mean teaching all of it.
Simplicity is a sustainability test: any approach, whether whole language, balanced or structured literacy, that is too complicated to do daily is not doable.
Teaching children to read and write well can reduce behavior problems, leaving more room for social-emotional learning.
Goldenberg's call to drop opaque language and agree on shared essentials is the way the science of reading movement can get unstuck.
quotes: Since we don’t get to choose our students, we teach the ones we have, not the ones we want—and since they come to us in many different ways, the teaching isn’t always so straightforward.

All readers learn to connect symbols with sounds and meanings in highly similar ways, because of how the brain is wired . . . Whole-word or discovery-based methods ignore the constraints of how the brain actually learns written language.

Marnie Ginsberg (Reading Simplified) believes we are teaching too much, and I agree. Marnie writes: [Anita Archer] gave the example of a teacher insisting that students needed to know the term diphthong when learning the /oi/ sound, pointing out that she had read proficiently for decades before encountering the word!

We need to seriously question the rationale behind what we’re teaching teachers. One colleague, looking downcast—in fact, downright dejected—had just come out of a training session that provided her with an 800-page sourcebook. Without questioning the value of the contents of this book (which comes from a reputable PD provider), the sheer heft is enough to send a teacher sprinting back to the printable handouts from Teachers Pay Teachers.

Anita Archer expresses her concerns like this: One of the things I’m concerned about a little bit with the science of reading—so many of you have taken classes—LETRS classes, AIMS classes, CORE classes, other classes on the science of reading . . . And that was to be certain that we had the best understanding of all of the aspects of language possible involved in reading. But it didn’t mean that we had to teach all of that to our students. And what I’m concerned about is that sometimes we are increasing the cognitive load that students have—that may actually slow the acquisition of reading.

Any reading approach—including Whole Language, Balanced Literacy, and Structured Literacy—that features elements that are unnecessarily complicated for teacher and student alike is not doable in the long-run.

I believe simplicity can save us because before you can pare something down you have to understand the thing you’re dealing with, the difference—as Anita Archer keeps reminding us—between the stuff and the fluff.
